docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: • This datasheet documents my individual work on Project Phoenix Phorse as part of RAS 304 at Arizona State University. It covers my block diagram, component selection, bill of materials, schematic, and power budget for the subsystem I am responsible for, so a reader can understand what I designed, why I chose each part, and how it fits into the full system.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
• Project Phoenix Phorse is a portable, rechargeable LiDAR system for robotic platforms. A laser distance sensor on a rotating mechanism scans 360 degrees to detect nearby obstacles, and a buzzer or speaker sounds an alert when an object comes within a set distance. The device is meant to be compact and energy-efficient so robotics companies can add it to existing robots.

  • My work supports this goal by [one sentence on your subsystem, e.g. "designing the portion of the system"]. The full project is described in the Team 105 report.

docs.title: Overvie
docs.text:
• Power source: A battery pack feeding protection and a power switch, then the voltage regulators. The battery chemistry and capacity are still TBD.
  • Power levels: VBAT (unregulated), plus the regulated rails VLOGIC, VSENSOR, VMOTOR, VAUDIO and VVIB, all with common ground. The voltages and currents are TBD.
  • Sensors: Only monitoring ones. A battery voltage divider and a current-sense amp feed the microcontroller's ADC pins, and it also reads a power-good signal and the power switch state. The LiDAR and other sensors belong to your teammates' boards.
  • Actuators: None driven directly except the two status LEDs and the per-board load switches. Indirectly, you power the other boards' actuators: the motor (VMOTOR), speaker (VAUDIO), vibration motor (VVIB) and laser/scanning (VSENSOR).
  • Team connections: Four separate power connectors: P1 to Data Collection, P2 to Laser/Scanning, P3 to Trigger, P4 to Interpretation. These are power only, not the J1–J3 data ribbons.
  • Control and safety: The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano turns each board's power on and off separately and reports faults on the LEDs. The protection stage guards the battery and the boards

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
Table 1: High-Side Current Sense Amplifier & Shunt (Power Subsystem)

High-Side Current Sense Amplifier & Shunt (Power Subsystem)

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. INA180A1IDBVR Current Sense Amp$0.85/eachDigi-Key product page: INA180A1IDBVR · TI datasheet * Wide common-mode input range (2.7V to 26V) independent of supply* High accuracy with low offset voltage (150 µV max)* Compact SOT-23-5 package saves PCB space * Requires precise, low-value external current shunt resistor* Fixed gain variant must be selected at purchase. Option 2. MAX44284EAUT+T Current Sense Amp$1.42/eachAnalog Devices product page: MAX44284 · datasheet * Ultra-low supply current consumption (21 µA)* Extremely low input offset voltage for high precision* Wide dynamic operating range * Higher unit cost compared to Texas Instruments alternatives* Potential supply chain lead time fluctuations

Choice: Option 1: INA180A1IDBVR Current Sense Amp

Rationale: The INA180 offers an optimal balance of cost, high common-mode voltage handling, and factory-trimmed gain accuracy. Using a dedicated current-sense IC avoids the CMRR degradation common with discrete differential amplifier circuits while keeping the board layout compact.

Table 2: Voltage Regulators (Power Subsystem)

Voltage Regulators (Power Subsystem)

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. LM7805CT Linear Regulator$0.65/eachDigi-Key product page: LM7805CT/NOPB · TI datasheet * Simple implementation requiring minimal external capacitors* Robust internal thermal overload and short-circuit protection* Through-hole package is easy to prototype and solder * Low efficiency when stepping down from higher voltages (high thermal dissipation)* Fixed 5V output voltage only. Option 2. TPS54302DDCR Step-Down Buck Regulator$1.10/eachDigi-Key product page: TPS54302DDCR · TI datasheet * High power conversion efficiency (up to 95%) minimizing heat dissipation* Supports continuous output currents up to 3A* Adjustable output voltage via feedback resistors * Requires external inductor and filter capacitors (larger layout)* Surface-mount thermal pad requires careful soldering

Choice: Option 2: TPS54302DDCR Step-Down Buck Regulator

Rationale: Switching buck regulators like the TPS54302 are essential for our handheld system to prevent excessive power loss and thermal buildup compared to linear regulators, especially when dropping battery voltage down to logic and sensor levels.

Table 3: Protection / Power Switch (Power Subsystem)

Protection / Power Switch (Power Subsystem)

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. Rocker Power Switch (12V/10A)$1.20/eachLittelfuse / C&K rocker switch datasheet * High current handling capacity (>10A safely)* Clear tactile feedback for physical on/off user status* Panel-mount design secure against mechanical shock * Manual electromechanical switch (cannot be toggled via software)* Bulkier physical footprint on enclosure. Option 2. MAX17613 High-Voltage Overvoltage Protector IC$2.15/eachAnalog Devices product page: MAX17613 * Automatic electronic overvoltage and reverse-polarity protection* Integrated low-resistance MOSFET switch* Compact IC package * Higher component unit cost* Does not provide a physical mechanical disconnect

Choice: Option 1: Rocker Power Switch (12V/10A)

Rationale: A robust mechanical power switch provides an unmistakable master disconnect for the handheld battery pack, ensuring safety during transport and servicing while easily handling total system startup surge currents. |

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. 9V battery holder with switch & 5.5mm/2.1mm plug (12V/10A)$3.95/eachExternal battery for the product * This is best solution for the wireless * Panel-mount design secure against mechanical shock

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This page lists every part on the power board schematic (TEST_304.kicad_sch): input protection, an LM7805 logic rail, a TPS54302 5 V buck for the motor supply, low-side current sense, the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, UART ribbon, spare GPIO headers, debug LEDs and test points. The BOM was exported from KiCad (bom_csv_grouped_by_value); all parts are ordered from Digi-Key. Table 1 covers the PCB parts with 1 spare, and Table 2 adds a breadboard-compatible (through-hole or breakout) version of each part so the circuit can be tested before moving to the PCB. Unit prices are estimates at quantity 1 and will be confirmed at checkout.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The Curiosity Nano, 1N5822, LM7805 and 1x40 headers are already breadboard-compatible. XH connectors, IDC header and test points use plain 2.54 mm header pins on the breadboard (from the 1x40 strips).
  • The TPS54302 is SMD only; the SOT-23-6 adapter lets it be soldered onto a breadboard-friendly DIP footprint.
  • Items likely stocked in TECH 162 (resistors, capacitors, LEDs, headers, fuses) can be removed from the order after checking the parts closet.
  • Datasheets are to be saved in the repository's datasheets/ folder.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The power distribution board for a multi-board robotics project. It takes 9V from a barrel jack through a fuse and reverse-protection diode, then splits the power into three outputs:

5 V logic from a linear regulator, for the microcontroller and other boards’ electronics 5 V motor supply (up to 3 A) from a buck converter, for the motor board Raw input voltage passed through to any board that needs it A PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano runs the board. A current-sense circuit measures motor current through a shunt resistor and reads it on an ADC pin. The board also has a UART ribbon connector, spare GPIO headers, test points, a power LED, two debug LEDs, and a debounced switch.
